children: By Sarah Klearman
Venture firm Zero Infinity Partners says venture capital is entering a new era: software is out, infrastructure is in.
The firm has banked $156 million for a sophomore fund to prove its thesis.
The fund

New York-based ZIP closed the fund in early August, said founder and Managing Partner John Kwaak. The firm, which has so far made 19 investments out of the fund, is planning to back a total of 25 to 30 companies with the capital.

Kwaak, previously the head of transport and logistics investing for Morgan Stanley Infrastructure Partners, launched ZIP in 2022. (Zip sounds like the Korean word for "house" or "home," the firm said. Kwaak was born and raised in Seoul.) ZIP closed an inaugural $104 million fund in 2023 to target what it called "infratech."
Its limited partners include large financial institutions and family offices that built their wealth in industries like shipbuilding, rail and power, among others, Kwaak said.
ZIP typically writes between $1 million and $5 million first checks, Kwaak said. It will reserve half the fund for follow-ons.
The context
Kwaak said he founded ZIP because he thought venture investors lacked the same level of sector expertise as their private-equity counterparts-which don't back early-stage companies.

"You end up with this interesting phenomenon where all the people that can write early-stage checks have not done infra and physical world deals, and all the people that have been doing physical world infrastructure deals for the last 20, 30 years, and have all the expertise, have never done an early-stage check," Kwaak said. "It didn't matter 10 years ago, because there just weren't enough founders starting companies that necessitate somebody to pull from both worlds, but now it's clearly changed."

After a decade plus defined by software companies, venture-capital firms are turning their attention to technology with a physical component in sectors like defense, manufacturing and robotics. The infrastructure necessary to power the AI boom-energy and hardware to bring data centers online, for example-has also become a magnet for investment.

The value of global venture capital investment in infrastructure has risen over the last decade, according to data from PitchBook. Investment in that category-which PitchBook defines as companies that own physical assets necessary for the movement of goods, multimodal commerce or power generation-is at $9.34 billion year-to-date as of Wednesday, up from $969 million in 2016. Elon Musk's tunnel builder The Boring Co. and chip company Cerebras Systems, which closed $3 billion and $1 billion funding rounds this year, respectively, account for two of the top deals in the category over the last decade, according to PitchBook.
The strategy
ZIP wants to identify bottlenecks in various infrastructure systems and then back companies working to solve them, Kwaak said.

Portfolio company Metropolis, for example, uses computer vision to help its members find and pay for parking more easily. Metropolis's technology recognizes members' vehicles, allowing them to park at its network of lots and garages without a physical transaction for payment.

ZIP participated in Metropolis's 2022 Series B, a $167 million round it raised at an undisclosed valuation. Last year, Metropolis announced it raised a $500 million Series D round as part of a larger financing that valued the company at about $5 billion.
Metropolis co-founder and Chief Executive Alex Israel said Kwaak was early to understand his company's vision of applying frontier technology to existing physical assets.

Roughly a quarter of ZIP's portfolio companies fall into the aviation infrastructure sector, Kwaak said. It has also invested in infrastructure for the midstream stage of the metals supply chain and in artificial-intelligence infrastructure, among other sectors. Kwaak said ZIP's focus on AI infrastructure has become more selective as valuations of companies in that sector have increased.

The conventional playbook of venture-backed companies-to move fast and break things-doesn't apply to infratech, where the cost of failure might be a grid outage or a hundred-million-dollar construction delay, ZIP wrote in a memo published this year. The firm believes the category can generate venture-scale returns nonetheless.
Kwaak said ZIP's first fund is performing "very positively," but declined to disclose performance metrics. The fund hasn't yet had an exit.
